title: What the Coldcard Vulnerability Reveals About Single Points of Failure
summary: A firmware flaw left Coldcard seeds weak for five years and cost owners about $116M. See why single points of failure matter and how multi-key custody changes the risk.
body_markdown:
## Key Takeaways


-


The 2026 Coldcard vulnerability highlights the need for multi-sig and custodial solutions to protect assets.


-


Multi-sig eliminates single points of failure.


-


The incident shows why effective crypto custody depends on independent key generation, separated signing authority, and controls that can withstand individual failures.


Hardware wallets have become a cornerstone of bitcoin self-custody because they keep private keys isolated from internet-connected devices. Owners can store bitcoin for years, authorize transactions offline, and retain direct control without relying on an exchange or custodian.


The 2026 Coldcard hack exposed a weakness in that security model. A firmware error introduced years earlier weakened the randomness used to generate wallet seeds. Some keys were vulnerable from creation, even as the devices continued operating normally. Owners had little indication that their bitcoin was at risk until attackers began moving funds.


## The Coldcard Hack: Five Years of Hidden Exposure


On July 30, 2026, attackers began draining bitcoin from wallets generated using vulnerable Coldcard firmware. By August 5,[preliminary estimates](https://www.trmlabs.com/resources/blog/the-largest-hardware-wallet-exploit-of-2026-inside-the-usd-116-million-coldcard-hack) put losses at approximately 1,816 BTC, then worth nearly $116 million. The thefts involved more than 5,200 addresses across at least four waves of activity.


The vulnerability originated in a March 2021 firmware release. A build and integration error caused affected devices to use a non-cryptographic software random number generator during seed creation, making some resulting keys vulnerable to reconstruction according to Coinkite.


The manufacturer's[technical investigation](https://blog.coinkite.com/entropy-technical-backgrounder/) estimated that affected Mk2 and Mk3 wallets had approximately 40 bits of effective security, while Mk4, Mk5, and Q wallets had roughly 72 bits, compared with the intended 128 bits. Each additional bit doubles the number of possible combinations an attacker must search. Reducing security from 128 to 40 bits shrank that search from an effectively impossible task to roughly one trillion possibilities, making some private keys feasible to guess. The 72-bit wallets were harder to crack but still significantly weaker than intended.


Many affected owners had been using their wallets as intended.[Research into the compromised holdings](https://crypto.jobs/news/coldcard-hardware-wallet-breach-reaches-115m-as-galaxy-research-tracks-over-200-victims) found that approximately 88% of the compromised bitcoin had remained untouched for at least a year. The average affected holding had been dormant for roughly three and a half years.The unfortunate target of this attack were normal bitcoin holders who were following the long shared advice of using a hardware wallet.


## How the Coldcard Entropy Flaw Compromised Private Keys


Bitcoin wallets derive private keys from a seed. The unpredictability of the data used to create that seed, known as entropy, helps determine how difficult it is for an attacker to reproduce the keys.


Secure seed generation creates an enormous number of possibilities, making a search computationally impractical. Weak randomness can narrow that search substantially, which is why many self-custody holders will roll dice to generate sufficient entropy for a truly random seed.


In Coldcard's case, a build and link integration error routed seed generation to MicroPython's non-cryptographic random number generator instead of the intended hardware source. The hardware generator had not failed, and the software generator was not an intentional backup for seed creation. Block's[root-cause analysis](https://engineering.block.xyz/blog/predictable-rng-fallback-and-32-bit-reseed-in-coldcard-firmware) explains how the integration and reseeding behavior weakened the seeds.


Each bit of effective entropy doubles the number of possibilities an attacker must search. Reducing that search space from 128 bits to approximately 40 bits can make key reconstruction feasible. A 72-bit search space also represents a substantial reduction, although exploitation depends on the wallet configuration and attack method.


Weak seeds still produce valid bitcoin addresses and sign transactions normally. Everyday use may reveal nothing about the underlying vulnerability.


### Why a Firmware Update Is Not Enough


Corrected firmware repairs future seed generation, but it does not repair an existing weak seed. Affected holders need to follow the manufacturer's migration guidance and move funds to securely generated replacement keys. For bitcoin holders who weren't actively monitoring security disclosures, the warning could come too late. Those who failed to move their funds before attackers exploited their vulnerable keys risked losing their bitcoin.


The[technical guidance](https://blog.coinkite.com/entropy-technical-backgrounder/) distinguishes seeds supplemented with at least 50 fair, independent, private dice rolls, which Coinkite does not consider vulnerable to this flaw alone. A strong, unique BIP-39 passphrase can reduce exposure, but does not repair the seed.


## Why the Vulnerability Went Undetected


The Coldcard vulnerability remained in publicly available firmware for more than five years. Although outside researchers could examine the code, the flaw went undetected until attackers began exploiting it in 2026. Making code available for inspection does not guarantee that every vulnerability will be found.


The investigation also evolved.[Initial warnings](https://theblock.co/post/410235/coinkite-coldcard-mk3-warning) focused on Mk3 devices, while later analysis expanded the scope of affected models.


The incident has prompted scrutiny of hardware wallet testing and disclosure practices.[Independent entropy validation](https://encapsulate.xyz/blog/what-broke-coldcards-bitcoin-security) can help identify weaknesses in key generation, while[outside security research](https://cointelegraph.com/magazine/does-the-coldcard-attack-mean-all-hardware-wallets-are-now-insecure) can uncover vulnerabilities that internal testing misses.


For institutions, the lesson extends beyond hardware wallets. Security depends on how key generation is tested, how vulnerabilities are disclosed, and which safeguards remain when a control fails.


## Single-Signature vs. Multi-sig: Why Independent Keys Matter


The consequences of a compromised private key depend on the wallet architecture surrounding it. In a single-signature bitcoin wallet, one private key can authorize transactions. If an attacker reconstructs that key, they can move the funds it controls without accessing the hardware device.


This creates a single point of failure: those funds depend on one key and the process that generated it. Multi-signature wallets distribute signing authority across multiple keys. In a two-of-three arrangement, any two of three authorized keys must sign a transaction. Compromising one key is insufficient to spend the bitcoin.


If only one Coldcard-generated key is compromised and the other keys remain secure, an attacker still needs another key to authorize a transfer.


### How Multi-sig Helped During the Coldcard Exploit


More than[10,000 BTC were moved out of affected Coldcard multi-sig wallets](https://foundation.mara.com/articles/peter-todd-joins-mara-foundation-slipstream) through Slipstream, according to the MARA Foundation. Multi-sig gave some owners time to respond, but protection depended on how many keys were vulnerable.


Transaction handling also mattered. Spending from common bitcoin multi-sig outputs reveals the spending script and its public keys. Broadcasting that transaction to the public mempool makes this information available before confirmation.


Public keys do not ordinarily expose private keys. In this exploit, however, they could help attackers identify keys derived from weak seeds. If attackers reconstructed enough keys to meet the signing threshold, they could attempt a competing transaction before the owner's transfer was confirmed. A two-of-three wallet with two vulnerable Coldcard keys could therefore remain at risk even if its third key was generated independently.


A[private transaction recovery process](https://foundation.mara.com/articles/9k-bitcoin-rescued-out-of-coldcard-multisigs) lets owners submit transfers directly to MARA for mining without first broadcasting them to the public mempool. Transaction details became public after confirmation.


Multi-sig and private submission addressed different risks. Multi-sig required attackers to compromise enough keys to authorize a spend. Private submission reduced the opportunity to exploit newly revealed wallet information before a recovery transaction was confirmed.


### Independence Matters More Than the Number of Keys


Multi-sig protects against compromise of fewer keys than the signing threshold requires. It cannot protect a wallet if an attacker obtains enough keys, including through a flaw shared by multiple signers.


A two-of-three wallet may be compromised if two keys share the same vulnerability. Separate keys also offer limited protection when their backups, credentials, or administrative controls are concentrated in one location or person.


Effective multi-sig requires independent key generation, secure storage, and separation of signing authority. The practical question is whether one failure could compromise enough keys to authorize a transfer.


## Who Bears the Risk When Security Fails?


Self-custody gives bitcoin holders direct control over their assets. It also makes them responsible for key management, backups, software updates, and recovery.


The Coldcard incident exposed a difficult limitation of that arrangement. Owners could follow established security practices while relying on a key-generation process they had no practical way to verify. Some lost funds despite using their wallets as intended.


The incident has raised questions about manufacturer accountability.[Legal analysis of the incident](https://www.fieldfisher.com/en/insights/coinkite-coldcard-hack-what-victims-need-to-know) examines potential claims, while[reporting on proposed litigation](https://news.bitcoin.com/coinkite-faces-class-action-threat-as-bitcoin-wallet-bug-costs-users-over-1300-btc/) describes differing views about whether affected owners could recover damages. Liability and recovery remain uncertain.


[Regulated custody](https://www.bitgo.com/resources/blog/qualified-custody-vs-self-custody/?utm_source=blog&utm_medium=custody&utm_campaign=coldcard_vulnerability_reveals) places asset safeguarding and key management with a specialized provider. It changes who manages those responsibilities and how security controls are monitored and governed, while introducing reliance on the custodian.

## Frequently Asked Questions


### What caused the 2026 Coldcard hack?


A firmware build and integration error introduced in March 2021 routed seed generation to a non-cryptographic software random number generator. Attackers exploited the weakened seeds to reconstruct some private keys.


### Which Coldcard devices were affected?


Affected releases included Mk2 and Mk3 firmware versions 4.0.1 through 4.1.9 and certain Mk4, Mk5, and Q releases. Owners should consult the[current security advisory](https://blog.coinkite.com/coldcard-mk3-seed-generation-warning/) and its linked model-specific guidance.


### Can a hardware wallet be hacked without physical access?


Yes. If a wallet generates predictable keys, attackers may be able to reconstruct them without accessing the device or obtaining its recovery phrase.


### Does updating Coldcard firmware protect existing wallets?


Updating firmware corrects future seed generation. It does not repair an existing weak seed. Affected holders should follow the manufacturer's guidance for securely generating replacement keys and transferring funds.


### Would multi-sig have prevented the Coldcard exploit?


Multi-sig can prevent theft when attackers compromise fewer keys than the signing threshold requires. A two-of-three wallet remains vulnerable if attackers reconstruct two keys. During recovery, public mempool exposure could also help attackers identify vulnerable keys before a transfer is confirmed.


### How does qualified custody reduce crypto custody risk?


Qualified custody places key management and asset safeguarding with a regulated custodian. BitGo combines cold storage, multi-key signing, transaction policies, and operational oversight to reduce reliance on individual devices and operators. Customers rely on the custodian to maintain those protections.
